An executor is simply a person (or thing) that carries out, performs, or puts into effect a task, a plan, or a set of instructions. Think of the word "execute" — it means to do something, to carry it out. An executor is the one who does that carrying out.

The word is used in a few different areas of life, and understanding each one will give you a complete picture.
1. The Legal Meaning (Most Important and Most Common)

This is by far the most widely used meaning, and the one you are most likely to encounter.

When a person dies, they often leave behind a will — a legal document that says things like "I want my house to go to my daughter" or "I want my savings divided equally among my three children." A will is essentially a set of instructions written by someone for after their death.

But here's the thing: a dead person cannot carry out their own instructions. Someone alive and trustworthy needs to step in and actually do all the work of making those wishes happen. That person is the executor.

So, an executor is:

A person who is named in someone's will — or appointed by a court — to manage and settle that person's affairs after they die, according to the instructions in the will.

What does an executor actually do?

The job is substantial. An executor typically has to:

  • Locate and read the will to understand what the deceased person wanted.
  • Notify the relevant authorities — such as banks, government agencies, and courts — that the person has died.
  • Go through probate, which is the legal process by which a court officially validates the will and gives the executor the legal authority to act on behalf of the deceased person's estate.
  • Gather and protect the deceased's assets — this includes money in bank accounts, property, investments, vehicles, jewelry, and anything else of value that the person owned.
  • Pay outstanding debts and taxes — before anything is distributed to anyone, the estate's debts (like unpaid bills or loans) and any taxes owed must be settled first.
  • Distribute what remains to the people named in the will (called beneficiaries) according to the instructions.
  • Keep detailed records of everything they do, because they are legally accountable for managing the estate properly.

Who can be an executor?

An executor is usually someone the deceased person trusted deeply — a spouse, an adult child, a close friend, or a professional like a lawyer or accountant. The person writing the will (called the testator) typically chooses their executor while they are still alive and names them directly in the will. The chosen person's consent is important — you cannot force someone to be an executor.

What if no executor is named, or the named executor cannot serve?

If a will doesn't name an executor, or if the named executor has died, refuses the role, or is otherwise unable to perform it, a court will step in and appoint someone to do the job. This court-appointed person is called an administrator rather than an executor, but the job they do is essentially the same.

A key concept: The Fiduciary Duty

An executor has what is called a fiduciary duty. This is a legal obligation to act honestly, carefully, and entirely in the best interests of the estate and its beneficiaries — not in their own personal interest. If an executor mismanages assets, steals from the estate, or shows favoritism, they can be held legally responsible and even sued.

A side note on gender

Historically, the female form of the word was executrix. However, in modern usage — especially in legal and professional contexts — executor is now widely used for any gender, and "executrix" is increasingly rare.

Outside of legal contexts, "executor" can refer more broadly to any person who carries out or puts into practice a plan, idea, strategy, or command.

For example:

  • A military general might be described as the executor of a battle plan.
  • A manager might be described as the executor of a company's strategy.
  • A contractor might be the executor of an architect's vision.

In this sense, the word simply highlights that the person is the one doing the work of turning instructions or plans into reality. This usage is more formal and less common in everyday speech, but perfectly correct.

In technology and software, an executor refers to a program, process, or component that is responsible for running or executing tasks — that is, carrying out instructions given to it.

For example, in programming frameworks, an executor might be a background service that takes a list of tasks and runs them one by one, or all at once in parallel. The idea is the same: it is the thing that carries out the work.

No matter which context you see the word in, the meaning is always rooted in the same idea: an executor is the one who makes things happen — who takes instructions, a plan, or a set of duties and actually carries them out.

In daily life, you will almost always see this word in its legal sense — the person responsible for handling a deceased person's estate and making sure their final wishes are fulfilled.

• "She was named the executor of her father's will and spent several months settling his estate."
  • "Without a reliable executor, the distribution of assets after death can become chaotic and contentious."
  • "The general acted as the executor of the battle plan, coordinating every unit precisely."
  • "In software, the task executor processes each job in the queue automatically."
